proof_text:
Let $p, q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p < q$. We define their midpoint
(arithmetic mean) as: $$ r = (p + q) \cdot 2^{-1} = \frac{p + q}{2} $$
where $2 = 1 + 1 \in \mathbb{Q}$. Since $1 > 0$, we have $2 > 0$, and
in any ordered field, the multiplicative inverse of a strictly
positive element is strictly positive, so $2^{-1} > 0$.

First, since $p < q$, adding $p$ to both sides gives:
$$ p + p < p + q \implies 2 \cdot p < p + q $$ Multiplying both sides
by $2^{-1} > 0$ preserves the strict inequality:
$$ p = (2 \cdot p) \cdot 2^{-1} < (p + q) \cdot 2^{-1} = r $$

Second, adding $q$ to both sides of $p < q$ gives:
$$ p + q < q + q \implies p + q < 2 \cdot q $$ Multiplying both sides
by $2^{-1} > 0$ yields:
$$ r = (p + q) \cdot 2^{-1} < (2 \cdot q) \cdot 2^{-1} = q $$

Combining these results, we obtain $p < r < q$. Since the rationals
are closed under addition and multiplication by reciprocals,
$r \in \mathbb{Q}$. Thus the rational order is dense: between any two
distinct rational numbers lies an intermediate rational.

then:

  suchThat:
  . p \:rational.less?:/ r
  . r \:rational.less?:/ q

                number."
